title: Making plans together
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A verb ending in -āmaḥ means 'we': gacchāmaḥ is 'we go', khādāmaḥ is 'we eat', paśyāmaḥ is 'we see'. L1 taught -mi for 'I' and -ti for 'he, she, your honour', and this is the third person-marking the course opens. It is built on the same stem those two were built on, so nothing about the verb changes except its last syllable.

A suggestion is carried by the QUESTION, not by a special form of the verb. kim gacchāmaḥ? is 'shall we go?', and gacchāmaḥ on its own is 'we are going'. The same three words do statement and proposal; only kim and the rise at the end tell them apart.

A grammar book will offer gacchema for 'let us go' — the optative, a whole mood with its own set of endings. This course writes it NOWHERE, in this module or any other. Everyday spoken Sanskrit proposes a plan in the plain present, and reaching for the optative here buys a paradigm the course cannot explain and does not need.

kadā asks 'when'. It stands where the answer will stand, exactly as kutra and kim have since L1-M2, and the answers cost nothing at all: adya, śvaḥ, prātaḥ, sāyam and pratidinam are all L1's words and none of them takes an ending.

There is no clock in this course yet. 'At six' and 'half past four' need a numeral system this module cannot afford beside a new person-ending, so a time is settled as a part of the day — prātaḥ, sāyam — and the hour waits for a later level.
'With me' is mayā saha: the by-ending M4 opened, sitting on the person, and saha AFTER it. There is no preposition in the phrase and there is nothing in front of mayā.

saha is POSTPOSITIVE — it follows the word it belongs to — which is the placement law L1-M10 taught for ca and this module simply reuses. mayā saha, never saha mayā, for the same reason it is pustakam phalam ca and never ca phalam.
mayā is the 'by me, with me' shape of aham. L1-M1's row gave aham, mama ('my') and mahyam ('to me'); this is the fourth shape of that one word, and it is the shape saha reaches for.

astu closes a plan in one word: 'let it be', 'agreed', 'fine'. It is the same verb as L1-M3's asti with the -tu ending every request in this level carries — asti reports that something IS, astu accepts that it will be.

vayam is 'we', and you will hear it far less than English 'we'. The -āmaḥ ending has already said who is going, so the bare gacchāmaḥ is the normal shape and vayam is added only for weight or contrast — the same economy L1-M10 spent a whole rule on for aham.

words.note: 'When'. It sits at the front, where the answer will sit, exactly as kutra does. L1 taught six question words and deliberately held this one back until there was a module that needed it.
M2's verb of going with the 'we' ending on it. That module taught gacchati, gacchāmi and the past and future shapes; -āmaḥ is new here, and it is the whole delta of this module.
Nobody is named in this question and nobody needs to be. The ending has already said that the speaker is one of the people going.

sentences.trap: English cannot ask this in two words. 'When shall we go?' needs a helper verb before it can propose anything, and here the plain present does the whole job with a question word in front of it.
sentences.sound: ka-DAA GACH-chhaa-mah. The -chchh- of gacchāmaḥ is one long held cluster, and the final -aḥ is a light breath, not a syllable of its own.

variations.cue: When shall we go to the school?
variations.changed: a destination is added in the bare accusative M6 taught, and the question around it does not move

variations.cue: When are you going?
variations.changed: the question is asked OF somebody instead of about us both, so the ending goes back to the third person

variations.cue: Where shall we go?
variations.changed: kadā gives way to M2's kutra — the two words occupy the same slot and ask different halves of the same plan

mistake.why: gacchema is the optative, the mood a grammar offers for 'let us go'. It is a real form and this course writes it nowhere: the suggestion is already in the question, and gacchāmaḥ is what a speaker says.

sentences.usage: The question that starts a plan, and often the whole of somebody's first turn.
sentences.mnemonic: -mi is me, -ti is that one, -maḥ is the two of us and anyone else coming.

sentences.cue: We are going to the school tomorrow.

words.note: 'We'. Written here once so that a learner has met it, and dropped in almost every other sentence of the module — the -āmaḥ ending has already said it.
M6's school in the shape a destination takes. Nothing about that shape changes because the verb now has two people in it.
M6's 'tomorrow', unchanged and unchangeable — a time word in this course takes no ending at all.

sentences.sound: va-YAM SHVAH vid-YAA-la-yam GACH-chhaa-mah. śvaḥ is one syllable: the sh and the v run together with nothing between them.

variations.cue: We are going to the school tomorrow.
variations.changed: vayam drops and the sentence means exactly the same thing — this is the normal shape, and the one above is the emphatic one

variations.cue: We are going home today.
variations.changed: the day and the destination both change, and the ending carrying the two of us does not

variations.cue: I am going to the school tomorrow.
variations.changed: one person goes instead of two, so -maḥ becomes -mi and vayam becomes aham

sentences.usage: A plan stated rather than proposed — the answer to somebody else's kadā.

sentences.cue: Shall we go to the library today?

words.note: M2's question marker at the front, and it is the only thing separating a proposal from a statement here. Everything after it would be a plain report of what we are doing.
The same three syllables as the sentence before, doing a different act because kim is standing in front of them.
M7's library as a destination. A compound is one word and one row, so the whole of it takes the one ending at the end.

sentences.trap: There is no word here for 'shall'. English builds a proposal out of a helper verb; this language builds it out of a question marker and the ordinary present, and the two sentences differ by one small word at the front.

variations.cue: We are going to the library today.
variations.changed: kim drops and the proposal becomes a statement — the only change in the line

variations.cue: Shall we go to the library tomorrow?
variations.changed: the day moves and nothing else does, because a time word has no ending to move

variations.cue: Shall we go to the school today?
variations.changed: the destination changes and takes the same -am it took as a library

mistake.why: The library is left in its naming shape. A place you go TO takes the -am ending M6 opened, and the verb having two people in it changes nothing about that.

sentences.usage: The everyday proposal, and the sentence this module is really for.

words.note: The fourth shape of M1's aham: aham is 'I', mama is 'my', mahyam is 'to me', and mayā is 'by me'. It is the same -ā ending M4 put on yānena and mārgeṇa, on a person instead of a thing.
'With', and it stands AFTER the word it belongs to. That is the same placement law M10 taught for ca — it is mayā saha, and saha mayā is the English order put into Sanskrit words.
L2-M1's 'please come', unchanged. The invitation is a request, so it carries the -tu ending every request in this level carries.

sentences.trap: English puts 'with' in front of 'me' and this language puts it behind. Worse, the pronoun itself changes shape — it is not aham with a word after it, it is mayā, and the two changes happen together.
sentences.sound: kri-PA-yaa ma-YAA SA-ha aa-GACH-cha-tu. mayā is two beats with the long aa at the end, and saha is two short ones.

variations.cue: Please come with me.
variations.changed: kṛpayā drops and the invitation is exactly as courteous, because the courtesy was always in -tu

variations.cue: Please come to the school with me.
variations.changed: a destination is added, and mayā saha stays exactly where it was

variations.cue: Please come along with me.
variations.changed: M4's gacchatu replaces āgacchatu, so the movement is away rather than towards the speaker

mistake.why: saha has been put in front, where English puts 'with'. It is postpositive — it follows what it governs — for the same reason ca and api do, and an English speaker reaches for this order every time.

sentences.usage: The invitation itself, said to one person addressed as bhavān or bhavatī.
sentences.mnemonic: The little words that mean 'and', 'also' and 'with' all come after. Say the thing first, then say what you are doing to it.

sentences.cue: Please have the meal with me.

words.note: The same two words as the sentence before, in front of a different verb. mayā saha is a unit and it does not rearrange itself for whatever follows.
M5's offering shape, now carrying an invitation rather than a plate. Hosting and planning are built out of the same one ending.
M5's meal, the thing eaten. The by-ending is on the person, not on the food — those are two different jobs and two different endings.

sentences.sound: kri-PA-yaa ma-YAA SA-ha BHO-ja-nam KHAA-da-tu. Said as one line, with the smallest of pauses after saha.

variations.cue: Please eat with me.
variations.changed: M5's annam replaces the whole meal, and kṛpayā drops

variations.cue: Please have some water with me.
variations.changed: eating becomes drinking; mayā saha does not notice

variations.cue: Please sit with me.
variations.changed: L2-M1's upaviśatu takes no object at all, and mayā saha is still the whole of 'with me'

sentences.usage: An invitation to a meal rather than an offer of one — the difference from M5 is that the speaker is eating too.

sentences.cue: Shall we eat in the evening?

words.note: M4's verb of eating with the 'we' ending. It is built exactly as gacchāmaḥ is — the ending is the lesson, and it sits on any verb the course already teaches.
M4's 'in the evening'. This is as precise as a time gets in this course: there is no clock here, and a part of the day is what a plan is settled on.
M5's food, and still the thing eaten rather than the person eating. Nothing about it changes because two people are now doing the eating.

sentences.trap: sāyam is 'in the evening' and that is the whole of the time. A learner who wants to say 'at seven' is reaching for a numeral system this course has not built yet, and the honest plan is made out of parts of the day.
sentences.sound: KIM SAA-yam AN-nam khaa-DAA-mah. khādāmaḥ has two long aa vowels in a row and both are held.

variations.cue: We are eating in the evening.
variations.changed: kim drops and the proposal becomes the settled plan

variations.cue: Shall we eat in the morning?
variations.changed: M4's prātaḥ replaces sāyam — the other end of the day, and the same shape of sentence

variations.cue: Shall we have the meal in the evening?
variations.changed: vayam is written out for weight and the food becomes a whole meal

mistake.why: -mi is 'I'. This asks whether I, alone, shall eat — which is a strange question to put to somebody else. A joint plan needs the -maḥ ending.

sentences.usage: Settling the half of a plan that is about food, which in practice is most of it.

words.note: 'Let it be', and in a conversation about plans it is 'agreed'. It is M3's asti with the request ending: asti says something IS, astu accepts that it will be.
M4's 'in the morning', stacked after śvaḥ with no word between them. Two time words in a row simply narrow each other.
M6's 'tomorrow'. Together with prātaḥ it is as close to a time as this level gets, and it is close enough for a plan.

sentences.sound: AS-tu. SHVAH PRAA-tah GACH-chhaa-mah. astu is two quick beats and is usually said on its own before the rest follows.

variations.cue: Yes. We'll go tomorrow morning.
variations.changed: M2's ām agrees instead — ām answers a question, astu accepts a proposal, and here either will do

variations.cue: Agreed. We'll go in the evening.
variations.changed: the time is renegotiated in the same breath as the agreement

variations.cue: Agreed.
variations.changed: one word closes the plan and nothing else is needed, which is how a plan usually does close

sentences.usage: The word that ends the negotiation, said the moment the other person's suggestion is acceptable.
sentences.mnemonic: asti is 'it is'; astu is 'let it be'. One reports the world, the other agrees to it.

words.note: The same question word, now asked of one person rather than of us both. kadā does not change for who is being asked.
M2's polite 'you', still taking the third-person -ti verb. A module about 'we' does not disturb the register the course has spoken since M2.
The -ti ending, back for one sentence. Setting it beside gacchāmaḥ is the clearest way to hear what -āmaḥ is doing.

sentences.trap: The ending changed and the word order did not. English marks the difference between 'are you going' and 'are we going' with a different pronoun; here it is the last syllable of the verb, and the pronoun is usually not there at all.

variations.cue: When are you going home?
variations.changed: the person asked is a woman, so bhavān becomes bhavatī — and the verb does not move, because it never agreed with gender

variations.cue: When are you going home?
variations.changed: kadā moves in behind the subject; the question is the same one and the emphasis shifts slightly onto the person

variations.cue: I am going home in the evening.
variations.changed: the answer rather than the question, with the -mi ending because only one person is going

sentences.usage: Asked of the other person when the plan depends on their day rather than on yours.

sentences.cue: Shall we go and see the flowers?

words.note: M4's verb of seeing with the 'we' ending. It is the third and last -āmaḥ shape this module writes: the ending is the lesson, and a fourth verb in it would teach nothing new.
Written here for the second and last time in the module. Notice that the eight other sentences manage without it, which is the point.
M9's flowers, more than one of them. What is seen takes the same shape it takes as the thing that pleases you.

sentences.sound: KIM va-YAM push-PAA-ni pash-YAA-mah. The ṣ of puṣpāṇi and the ś of paśyāmaḥ are two different sh sounds; the first is made further back in the mouth.

variations.cue: Shall we see the flowers?
variations.changed: vayam drops, which is what nearly every real sentence does with it

variations.cue: We are looking at the flowers.
variations.changed: kim drops and the proposal becomes a report of what is happening

variations.cue: Do you see the flowers?
variations.changed: the question is put to the other person, so the ending goes back to -ti and the proposal becomes an ordinary question

sentences.usage: The kind of small suggestion a plan is actually made of, once the where and the when are settled.

sentences.display: kim śvaḥ pustakālayam gacchāmaḥ? ām, astu.
sentences.script: किम् श्वः पुस्तकालयम् गच्छामः? आम्, अस्तु।
sentences.cue: Shall we go to the library tomorrow? Yes, agreed.

words.note: The plan closing. Two words answer the whole proposal, and neither of them repeats a single word of it.
The ending this module exists for, in the sentence that shows what it is for: a proposal made and accepted in one exchange.
M2's 'yes', answering the kim. ām answers the question; astu accepts the plan — and a speaker very often says both.

sentences.trap: The answer contains no verb at all. English repeats something — 'yes, let's' — and this exchange closes on two indeclinable words, one of which is a verb form doing no verb's work.
sentences.sound: KIM SHVAH pus-ta-KAA-la-yam GACH-chhaa-mah? AAM, AS-tu. The answer is said quickly and lower than the question.

variations.cue: Shall we go to the library tomorrow? Agreed.
variations.changed: astu alone answers, which is the commonest reply of the two

variations.cue: Shall we go to the library today? Yes.
variations.changed: the day moves and the answer is the bare yes

variations.display: kim śvaḥ pustakālayam gacchāmaḥ? na, aham na gacchāmi.
variations.script: किम् श्वः पुस्तकालयम् गच्छामः? न, अहम् न गच्छामि।
variations.cue: Shall we go to the library tomorrow? No, I am not going.
variations.changed: the plan is declined, and the refusal drops to the -mi ending because it is only about the speaker

mistake.display: kim śvaḥ pustakālayam gacchāmaḥ? ām, asti.
mistake.why: asti reports that something exists — 'yes, it is' — which answers nothing that was asked. Agreeing to a plan is astu, with the same -tu ending every request in this level carries.

sentences.usage: The whole module in one exchange: a proposal carried by a question, and an agreement carried by one word.

comprehensionPool.cue: Please come to the library with me.
Agreed. We'll eat in the evening.
Shall we look at the book today?
When are you going to the school?
We go to the school every day.
Shall we go tomorrow evening? Yes.
Let my friend come with me.
When shall we go? We'll go in the morning.

comprehensionPool.display: astu, kintu aham adya na gacchāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: अस्तु, किन्तु अहम् अद्य न गच्छामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: Agreed, but I am not going today.
Rāma is going to the library with me.
We are looking at the beautiful flowers.
